criteria.rationale: Verified the standard CLI enables the run shim, fd 3 is not inherited, and dead-owner release requires a stalled marker. Unresolved assumptions are that the shim can inspect and signal every child and can publish its full report; N2 and N3 capture those failures. Accepted spec limits are shimless embedder environment matching (L6), non-Linux group-only cleanup (L2), external live-parent escape (L1), markerless legacy reservation confirmation (L4), and non-inspectable process handling (L3).
The run shim confines subreaper scope, but an inspection failure exits before the subtree is fully reaped and the dispatcher-only owner marker lets release proceed after dispatcher death.
The CLI additions are additive and a released reservation is represented as an ordinary failed run plus receipt; run/receipt schemas remain unchanged.
Attempt identifiers are validated, abandonment is a typed refusal, live owners are refused, and read/receipt failures retain context.
The change stays within pose-mcp and does not alter REST, MCP, protobuf, or event contracts. The integration assessment's unobserved HTTP consumers are outside the changed surface.
A report larger than the reader limit can block before the shim returns; truncated JSON produces a generic unreadable-report failure and loses the PIDs the run record should name.
Earlier run records retain their meaning; the new release writes the existing failed-run and receipt formats, and the CLI flag is additive.
An unbounded descendant list can block report publication and prevent a fully reaped run from completing its required record and conclusion path.

The process-scoped shim addresses the cause that process-group kills miss detached sessions while avoiding dispatcher-wide subreaper adoption and reviewer-controlled environment authority. The release records preserve ordinary run semantics. The design assessment observed no structural deltas; N2 and N3 are implementation gaps.
The root and localized manuals, scaffold copies, and runtime limitation text still describe environment-based cleanup as the normal path.
The documented cleanup guarantee and diagnostic limitations do not match the standard CLI's shim behavior, so operators cannot rely on the stated process-selection and disclosure behavior.
R2 is not met when the ended-PID report exceeds 64 KiB; N3 also leaves a process-liveness gap when cleanup fails after dispatcher death.
The implementation, tests and manual updates align with the spec's review cleanup and abandoned-attempt scope.
A reviewer descendant can remain alive after the shim's fail-fast inspection path while release proves only that the dispatcher has died.

A per-run subreaper shim is the smallest sufficient ownership boundary for detached descendants; a process-wide subreaper or reviewer-controlled environment matching would broaden authority. The shim and lock-file release follow D1/D2, but report bounds and cleanup-failure liveness still need correction.

findings.rationale: The manuals and recorded containment limits still describe environment matching and unreadable prior-process disclosure as the normal Linux path. The standard CLI instead uses the run shim's subtree; environment matching is only the shimless embedder fallback. Update the English and pt-BR manuals and scaffold copies, plus the safety limitation text.

findings.action: The parent reads at most 64 KiB from the shim report, while the shim writes the complete unbounded ended-PID list. For a large list the reader stops draining and the shim blocks after reaping; dispatch waits until timeout/WaitDelay, then parses truncated JSON and marks cleanup incomplete. A fully reaped run becomes unconcludable and loses the full PID report.

The first unreadable /proc stat aborts subtree reaping. If the dispatcher has died, PDEATHSIG reaches this fail-fast path and the shim can exit with run descendants still alive; the marker tracks only the dispatcher PID and abandoned-attempt release checks only that owner's liveness, so cancel can later release the attempt while a reviewer process remains.
